newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-KITE SHARES LEAD WITH HULBERT AT GREATER GREENSBORO CLASSIC.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-KITE SHARES LEAD WITH HULBERT AT GREATER GREENSBORO CLASSIC.

text.p: U.S. Ryder Cup captain Tom Kite took another small step towards playing his way onto his own team as he tied for the lead Friday after the second round at the Greater Greensboro Chrysler Classic.
Kite birdied three of his final five holes for a four-under-par 68 on the damp Forest Oaks course, where preferred lies were allowed for the second successive day.

He was joined at nine-under 135 by journeyman Mike Hulbert, who birdied his final three holes for a 69. Kite and Hulbert were one stroke better than fellow-Americans Mike Standly (68) and Kirk Triplett (69).

Kite, a distant second to Tiger Woods at the Masters a fortnight ago, is 28th in the U.S. Ryder Cup standings. The top 10 players after the PGA Championship in August automatically qualify for the U.S. team to play Europe on the Valderamma course in Sotogrande, Spain, September 26-28.
A victory this week would elevate Kite to just outside the top 10, but he strongly implied that he might not play in the Ryder Cup, even if he qualified.
Rather, he might prefer to use his own place on the team to give himself three captain's choices, rather than the usual two.
"I've got a long, long way to go," said Kite, who if he did play would be the first American playing-captain since Arnold Palmer in 1963.
"Making the team would afford me a lot of flexibility. It would give me some options (such as) stepping down and letting someone else play.
"One of the benefits of playing well is that I get paired with a lot of guys who are going to be on the team, so I have more of a first-hand awareness of what they're doing."
Kite's round was going nowhere until he got the putts to fall late. "It's a round I'm really proud of because I was so patient," he said.
"I had a lot of good opportunities I wasn't able to convert. I was playing wonderful golf and getting nothing out of it. That's frustrating."
Hulbert also was rewarded for his own patience as he ran in birdies from three, 15 and 10 feet respectively at his final three holes.

"I felt as though patience was my best club today," Hulbert said. "I said to my caddie 'let's birdie this final hole and play with captain Kite tomorrow'. I haven't played with captain Kite for a while."
Only eight strokes separated the 71 players who made the cut. Joint first-round leader Sandy Lyle survived without a shot to spare after parring his final four holes for a 77.
